cards.front: How do we see a light source, such as a lamp?
cards.back: Light from the object travels into our eyes.
cards.say: How do we see a light source, such as a lamp? Light from the object travels into our eyes.

cards.front: How do we see an object that is not a light source?
cards.back: Light from a source bounces off the object into our eyes.
cards.say: How do we see an object that is not a light source? Light from a source bounces off the object into our eyes.

cards.front: reflection
cards.back: Light bouncing off a surface.
cards.say: reflection. Light bouncing off a surface.

cards.front: Why is a mirror a good reflector?
cards.back: Its surface is very smooth and shiny, so light bounces off in a regular way.
cards.say: Why is a mirror a good reflector? Its surface is very smooth and shiny, so light bounces off in a regular way.

cards.front: normal
cards.back: An imaginary line at right angles to a surface where a ray meets it.
cards.say: normal. An imaginary line at right angles to a surface where a ray meets it.

cards.front: incident ray
cards.back: The ray of light that arrives at a surface.
cards.say: incident ray. The ray of light that arrives at a surface.

cards.front: reflected ray
cards.back: The ray of light that bounces off a surface.
cards.say: reflected ray. The ray of light that bounces off a surface.

cards.front: What is the law of reflection?
cards.back: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
cards.say: What is the law of reflection? The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

cards.front: Why can you not see yourself in a rough wall?
cards.back: It scatters light in many directions instead of reflecting it neatly.
cards.say: Why can you not see yourself in a rough wall? It scatters light in many directions instead of reflecting it neatly.

cards.front: How does a periscope work?
cards.back: It uses two mirrors to reflect light, so you can see over an obstacle.
cards.say: How does a periscope work? It uses two mirrors to reflect light, so you can see over an obstacle.

cards.front: refraction
cards.back: The bending of light when it passes from one material into another, such as from air to water.
cards.say: refraction. The bending of light when it passes from one material into another, such as from air to water.

cards.front: Why does a pencil in water look bent?
cards.back: Light bends as it leaves the water and enters the air.
cards.say: Why does a pencil in water look bent? Light bends as it leaves the water and enters the air.

cards.front: lens
cards.back: A curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light. A convex lens brings light together.
cards.say: lens. A curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light. A convex lens brings light together.

cards.front: Which kind of lens is used in a magnifying glass?
cards.back: A convex lens.
cards.say: Which kind of lens is used in a magnifying glass? A convex lens.

cards.front: prism
cards.back: A block of glass that splits white light into colours.
cards.say: prism. A block of glass that splits white light into colours.

cards.front: What are the colours of the spectrum in order?
cards.back: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
cards.say: What are the colours of the spectrum in order? Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

cards.front: Why do we see a rainbow?
cards.back: Raindrops refract and split sunlight into its colours.
cards.say: Why do we see a rainbow? Raindrops refract and split sunlight into its colours.

cards.front: How fast does light travel?
cards.back: About 300,000 kilometres each second.
cards.say: How fast does light travel? About three hundred thousand kilometres each second.

cards.front: pupil
cards.back: The hole in the middle of the eye that lets light in.
cards.say: pupil. The hole in the middle of the eye that lets light in.

cards.front: retina
cards.back: The layer at the back of the eye that detects light and sends signals to the brain.
cards.say: retina. The layer at the back of the eye that detects light and sends signals to the brain.

cards.front: Why does the pupil get smaller in bright light?
cards.back: To let in less light and protect the retina.
cards.say: Why does the pupil get smaller in bright light? To let in less light and protect the retina.

cards.front: Why does a red shirt look red?
cards.back: It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours.
cards.say: Why does a red shirt look red? It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours.

cards.front: Why does a white object look white?
cards.back: It reflects all the colours of light.
cards.say: Why does a white object look white? It reflects all the colours of light.

cards.front: Why does a black object look black?
cards.back: It absorbs nearly all the light, and very little is reflected.
cards.say: Why does a black object look black? It absorbs nearly all the light, and very little is reflected.
